items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose that [MATH: D] is an [MATH: n]th-order differential operator, and the functions [MATH: y, y_1,] and [MATH: y_2] are [MATH: n]-times differentiable in some domain of interest.

Content:
We say that a differential operator [MATH: D] is linear if the following conditions hold:

Content:
1. [MATH: D(a y(x)) = a D(y(x)),] where [MATH: a] is a constant.
2. [MATH: D(y_1(x) + y_2(x)) = D(y_1(x)) + D(y_2(x)).]

Content:
We can combine these two conditions into a single condition as follows:

Content:
[MATH: D(ay_1(x) + by_2(x)) = aD(y_1(x)) + bD(y_2(x))]
where [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are constants.

Content:
It's worth taking a moment to compare these conditions to those we used when defining a linear transformation
[MATH: \mathbf T: \mathbf v \rightarrow \mathbf w.]

Content:
For [MATH: \mathbf T] to be linear, it must satisfy the following conditions:

Content:
- [MATH: \mathbf{T}(a\mathbf{v})=a\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})] for any vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}] and any scalar [MATH: a.]
- [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1+\mathbf{v}_2)=\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1)+\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_2)] for any vectors [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2.]

Content:
The conditions are essentially the same in both cases! Only instead of a transformation [MATH: \mathbf T,] we have a differential operator [MATH: D.] And instead of vectors as our inputs and outputs, we have functions.

Content:
Next, we'll apply this definition to a specific differential operator to see if it is linear.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
For any linear differential operator [MATH: L,] we have the linearity condition [MATH: L(ay_1 + by_2) = aL(y_1) + bL(y_2)] for functions [MATH: y_1(x), y_2(x),] and where [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are constants.

For the given differential operator, we have

[MATH: D(ay_{1} + by_{2})|= (ay_{1} + by_{2})(d^{2})/(dx^{2})(ay_{1} + by_{2}) + (d)/(dx)(ay_{1} + by_{2}); = (ay_{1} + by_{2})(a(d^{2}y_{1})/(dx^{2}) + b(d^{2}y_{2})/(dx^{2})) + a(dy_{1})/(dx) + b(dy_{2})/(dx); = + a^{2}y_{1}(d^{2}y_{1})/(dx^{2}) + aby_{1}(d^{2}y_{2})/(dx^{2}) + aby_{2}(d^{2}y_{1})/(dx^{2}) + b^{2}y_{2}(d^{2}y_{2})/(dx^{2}); = + a(dy_{1})/(dx) + b(dy_{2})/(dx); = a^{2}y_{1}(d^{2}y_{1})/(dx^{2}) + b^{2}y_{2}(d^{2}y_{2})/(dx^{2}) + a(dy_{1})/(dx) + b(dy_{2})/(dx); = + ab(y_{1}(d^{2}y_{2})/(dx^{2}) + y_{2}(d^{2}y_{1})/(dx^{2})).]

This is not the same as the right-hand side, because [MATH: aD(y_{1}) + bD(y_{2})|= a[y_{1}(d^{2}y_{1})/(dx^{2}) + (dy_{1})/(dx)] + b[y_{2}(d^{2}y_{2})/(dx^{2}) + (dy_{2})/(dx)]; = ay_{1}(d^{2}y_{1})/(dx^{2}) + by_{2}(d^{2}y_{2})/(dx^{2}) + a(dy_{1})/(dx) + b(dy_{2})/(dx).]

Therefore, since [MATH: D(ay_1+by_2) \neq aD(y_1) + bD(y_2),] the operator [MATH: D] is nonlinear.

items.title: The General Form of a Linear Differential Operator

sections.normalized_html: An [MATH: n]th-order linear differential operator, denoted [MATH: L], has the general form: [MATH: L(y) = f_{n}(x)\dfrac{\textrm d^{n}y}{\textrm d x^{n}} + f_{n-1}(x)\dfrac{\textrm d^{n-1}y}{\textrm d x^{n-1}} + \cdots + f_{1}(x)\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm d x} + f_0(x)y.] The functions [MATH: f_i(x)] are called the coefficient functions. They must depend only on the variable [MATH: x] and be continuous on the domain of interest. The order of the operator is the order of the highest derivative whose coefficient is not zero.
sections.readable_text:
An [MATH: n]th-order linear differential operator, denoted [MATH: L], has the general form:
[MATH: L(y) = f_{n}(x)\dfrac{\textrm d^{n}y}{\textrm d x^{n}} + f_{n-1}(x)\dfrac{\textrm d^{n-1}y}{\textrm d x^{n-1}} + \cdots + f_{1}(x)\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm d x} + f_0(x)y.]
The functions [MATH: f_i(x)] are called the coefficient functions. They must depend only on the variable [MATH: x] and be continuous on the domain of interest. The order of the operator is the order of the highest derivative whose coefficient is not zero.

sections.normalized_html: If all the coefficient functions [MATH: f_i(x)] are constants, we call the operator a linear operator with constant coefficients.
sections.readable_text: If all the coefficient functions [MATH: f_i(x)] are constants, we call the operator a linear operator with constant coefficients.

sections.normalized_html: Let's look at two examples:
sections.readable_text: Let's look at two examples:

sections.normalized_html:
1. The operator [MATH: L(y) = x^2 y'' - (\sin x) y' + 2y] is a 2nd-order linear differential operator. Its coefficient functions are [MATH: f_2(x) = x^2], [MATH: f_1(x) = -\sin x], and [MATH: f_0(x) = 2].

  2. The operator [MATH: L(y) = 4y''' + 7y'' - y] is a 3rd-order linear operator with constant coefficients. Its coefficient functions are [MATH: f_3(x) = 4], [MATH: f_2(x) = 7], [MATH: f_1(x) = 0], and [MATH: f_0(x) = -1].

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that [MATH: D] is an [MATH: n]th-order differential operator, and the functions [MATH: y, y_1,] and [MATH: y_2] are [MATH: n]-times differentiable in some domain of interest.

Content:
We say that a differential operator [MATH: D] is linear if the following conditions hold:

Content:
1. [MATH: D(a y(x)) = a D(y(x)),] where [MATH: a] is a constant.
2. [MATH: D(y_1(x) + y_2(x)) = D(y_1(x)) + D(y_2(x)).]

Content:
We can combine these two conditions into a single condition as follows:

Content:
[MATH: D(ay_1(x) + by_2(x)) = aD(y_1(x)) + bD(y_2(x))]
where [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are constants.

Content:
It's worth taking a moment to compare these conditions to those we used when defining a linear transformation
[MATH: \mathbf T: \mathbf v \rightarrow \mathbf w.]

Content:
For [MATH: \mathbf T] to be linear, it must satisfy the following conditions:

Content:
- [MATH: \mathbf{T}(a\mathbf{v})=a\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v})] for any vector [MATH: \mathbf{v}] and any scalar [MATH: a.]
- [MATH: \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1+\mathbf{v}_2)=\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_1)+\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{v}_2)] for any vectors [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2.]

Content:
The conditions are essentially the same in both cases! Only instead of a transformation [MATH: \mathbf T,] we have a differential operator [MATH: D.] And instead of vectors as our inputs and outputs, we have functions.

Content:
Next, we'll apply this definition to a specific differential operator to see if it is linear.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: The Linearity Condition

Content:
A differential operator [MATH: D] is linear if the following linearity condition is satisfied.

Content:
[MATH: D(ay_1(x) + by_2(x)) = aD(y_1(x)) + bD(y_2(x))]
where [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are constants.

Content:
Let's consider some examples:

Content:
- First, let's consider the following differential operator:
[MATH: D_1(y) = x\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x} +x^2y]
This operator is indeed linear. To see this, we need to check that the linearity condition above holds. So we start by applying our operator to the function [MATH: y = a y_1(x) + b y_2(x){:}]
[MATH: D_{1}(ay_{1} + by_{2}) = x(d)/(dx)(ay_{1} + by_{2}) + x^{2}(ay_{1} + by_{2})]
Since derivatives distribute over sums, and [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are constants, we have
[MATH: D_{1}(ay_{1} + by_{2})|= x(d)/(dx)(ay_{1}) + x(d)/(dx)(by_{2}) + x^{2}(ay_{1} + by_{2}); = ax(d)/(dx)(y_{1}) + bx(d)/(dx)(y_{2}) + ax^{2}y_{1} + bx^{2}y_{2}; = a(x(dy_{1})/(dx) + x^{2}y_{1})_(⏟)_(D_{1}(y_{1})) + b(x(dy_{2})/(dx) + x^{2}y_{2})_(⏟)_(D_{1}(y_{2}))]
Thus, since [MATH: D_1(ay_1 + by_2) = aD_1(y_1) + bD_1(y_2),] the operator [MATH: D_1] is linear.

Content:
- Now, let's consider the following differential operator:
[MATH: D_2(y) = y\dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}]
This operator is not linear. To see this, we need to check that the linearity condition above does not hold. So we start by applying our operator to the function [MATH: y = a y_1(x) + b y_2(x){:}]
[MATH: D_{2}(ay_{1} + by_{2})|= (ay_{1} + by_{2})(d)/(dx)(ay_{1} + by_{2}); = (ay_{1} + by_{2})(a(dy_{1})/(dx) + b(dy_{2})/(dx)); = a^{2}y_{1}(dy_{1})/(dx) + aby_{1}(dy_{2})/(dx) + aby_{2}(dy_{1})/(dx) + b^{2}y_{2}(dy_{2})/(dx)]
Comparing this to [MATH: aD_2(y_1) + bD_2(y_2),] we see that they are not the same:
[MATH: aD_{2}(y_{1}) + bD_{2}(y_{2})|= ay_{1}(dy_{1})/(dx) + by_{2}(dy_{2})/(dx) ≠ D_{2}(ay_{1} + by_{2})]
Therefore, the operator [MATH: D_2] is not linear.

---

Item 3 — Example: Using the Properties of Linear Differential Operators to Identify Them

Example Prompt:
Show that the differential operator

[MATH: D(y) = y\dfrac{\textrm d^2 y}{\textrm d x^2} + \dfrac{\textrm d y}{\textrm d x}]

is nonlinear.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
For any linear differential operator [MATH: L,] we have the linearity condition
[MATH: L(ay_1 + by_2) = aL(y_1) + bL(y_2)]
for functions [MATH: y_1(x), y_2(x),] and where [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are constants.

For the given differential operator, we have

[MATH: D(ay_{1} + by_{2})|= (ay_{1} + by_{2})(d^{2})/(dx^{2})(ay_{1} + by_{2}) + (d)/(dx)(ay_{1} + by_{2}); = (ay_{1} + by_{2})(a(d^{2}y_{1})/(dx^{2}) + b(d^{2}y_{2})/(dx^{2})) + a(dy_{1})/(dx) + b(dy_{2})/(dx); = + a^{2}y_{1}(d^{2}y_{1})/(dx^{2}) + aby_{1}(d^{2}y_{2})/(dx^{2}) + aby_{2}(d^{2}y_{1})/(dx^{2}) + b^{2}y_{2}(d^{2}y_{2})/(dx^{2}); = + a(dy_{1})/(dx) + b(dy_{2})/(dx); = a^{2}y_{1}(d^{2}y_{1})/(dx^{2}) + b^{2}y_{2}(d^{2}y_{2})/(dx^{2}) + a(dy_{1})/(dx) + b(dy_{2})/(dx); = + ab(y_{1}(d^{2}y_{2})/(dx^{2}) + y_{2}(d^{2}y_{1})/(dx^{2})).]

This is not the same as the right-hand side, because
[MATH: aD(y_{1}) + bD(y_{2})|= a[y_{1}(d^{2}y_{1})/(dx^{2}) + (dy_{1})/(dx)] + b[y_{2}(d^{2}y_{2})/(dx^{2}) + (dy_{2})/(dx)]; = ay_{1}(d^{2}y_{1})/(dx^{2}) + by_{2}(d^{2}y_{2})/(dx^{2}) + a(dy_{1})/(dx) + b(dy_{2})/(dx).]

Therefore, since [MATH: D(ay_1+by_2) \neq aD(y_1) + bD(y_2),] the operator [MATH: D] is nonlinear.

---

Item 6 — Tutorial: The General Form of a Linear Differential Operator

Content:
An [MATH: n]th-order linear differential operator, denoted [MATH: L], has the general form:
[MATH: L(y) = f_{n}(x)\dfrac{\textrm d^{n}y}{\textrm d x^{n}} + f_{n-1}(x)\dfrac{\textrm d^{n-1}y}{\textrm d x^{n-1}} + \cdots + f_{1}(x)\dfrac{\textrm dy}{\textrm d x} + f_0(x)y.]
The functions [MATH: f_i(x)] are called the coefficient functions. They must depend only on the variable [MATH: x] and be continuous on the domain of interest. The order of the operator is the order of the highest derivative whose coefficient is not zero.

Content:
If all the coefficient functions [MATH: f_i(x)] are constants, we call the operator a linear operator with constant coefficients.

Content:
Let's look at two examples:

Content:
1. The operator [MATH: L(y) = x^2 y'' - (\sin x) y' + 2y] is a 2nd-order linear differential operator. Its coefficient functions are [MATH: f_2(x) = x^2], [MATH: f_1(x) = -\sin x], and [MATH: f_0(x) = 2].
2. The operator [MATH: L(y) = 4y''' + 7y'' - y] is a 3rd-order linear operator with constant coefficients. Its coefficient functions are [MATH: f_3(x) = 4], [MATH: f_2(x) = 7], [MATH: f_1(x) = 0], and [MATH: f_0(x) = -1].

For any linear differential operator [MATH: L,] we have

where [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are constants.

[MATH: L(2y_{1} − y_{2})|= 2L(y_{1}) − L(y_{2}); = 2\tan^{2} x − 2\sec^{2} x.]

[MATH: L(2y_{1} − y_{2})|= 2\tan^{2} x − 2(1 + \tan^{2} x); = − 2.]
